reason: The sources provide multi-source verification for over 10 distinct, engaging claims detailing Gemini 12's spacewalk breakthrough and radar-fail navigational recovery.
story: Before Gemini 12, walking in space was a dangerous failure. Early astronauts suffered extreme fatigue and overheating trying to work in zero gravity without adequate restraints. To solve this crisis, NASA introduced underwater neutral buoyancy training to simulate weightlessness. In November 1966, Gemini 12 launched with commander Jim Lovell and rookie Buzz Aldrin. When their primary rendezvous radar failed in orbit, Aldrin used a manual sextant and charts to calculate precise burn maneuvers to dock with an Agena target vehicle. During the mission, Aldrin performed three spacewalks totaling over five hours. Equipping himself with foot restraints, waist tethers, handrails, and strict rest intervals, he accomplished complex tasks with ease and zero overexertion. Gemini 12 finally proved humans could work safely outside a spacecraft, establishing the essential extravehicular techniques that made the Apollo Moon landings possible.
angle: Early spacewalks were so physically punishing that astronauts became dangerously exhausted, until Buzz Aldrin used underwater pool training and manual sextant math to master zero-gravity work on Gemini 12.

claims.claim: Gemini 12 was the tenth and final crewed mission of NASA's Project Gemini.
The Gemini 12 crew consisted of command pilot James A. Lovell Jr. and pilot Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin Jr.
Early Gemini spacewalkers suffered severe physical exhaustion and dangerous overheating due to a lack of proper foot and body restraints.
Underwater neutral buoyancy pool training was introduced to simulate zero-gravity spacewalk operations before Gemini 12.
Gemini 12 launched on November 11, 1966, from Cape Canaveral.
Gemini 12 rendezvoused and docked with an unpiloted Agena target vehicle launched about 90 minutes earlier.
When the onboard rendezvous radar failed, Buzz Aldrin used a sextant and analog charts to manually compute rendezvous maneuvers.
Buzz Aldrin completed three extravehicular activities during the Gemini 12 flight.
Aldrin accumulated over five hours of total spacewalking time during Gemini 12.
Aldrin used custom foot restraints, waist tethers, and planned rest periods to perform tasks without physical distress.
Gemini 12 successfully demonstrated that astronauts can safely work outside spacecraft, paving the way for the Apollo lunar landings.
Gemini 12 executed an automatically controlled reentry and splashed down in the Atlantic Ocean near the aircraft carrier USS Wasp.
Gemini 12 splashed down within 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) of its target recovery point.
Buzz Aldrin later became the second man on the Moon during Apollo 11, while Jim Lovell commanded Apollo 13.

disputed: Invention of underwater zero-g training: Popular books and films credit Aldrin with inventing underwater training, but historical research indicates neutral buoyancy testing originated with aerospace companies and NASA Langley prior to Gemini 12. Script handling: Attribute as 'While popular legend credits Aldrin with inventing underwater training, NASA and aerospace researchers had begun neutral buoyancy pool testing years earlier.'
